newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus falls 31 percent in August.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus falls 31 percent in August.

text.p: Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus dropped 31 percent in August from a year earlier and economists said a major reason for the decline was a big increase in oil imports.

The surplus fell to 369.47 billion yen ($3.35 billion), and the merchandise surplus with the United States -- often a source of friction between the two nations -- also declined 16.9 percent to 222.26 billion yen ($2.02 billion), the Ministry of Finance announced on Wednesday.
The figures were not adjusted for seasonal factors.
The August figure for the overall surplus represented a 21st consecutive month of year-on-year decline but was slightly higher than the top end of the range of analysts' forecasts.

A Reuters poll of analysts had shown the figure was expected to be between 160 billion yen ($1.45 billion) and 314 billion ($2.85 billion) after a 535.14 billion ($4.86 billion) surplus a year earlier.

"Japan's oil imports were up almost 15 percent year-on-year in June, so the recent increase in oil prices increased overall import value in Japan," said Susumu Kato, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo.

"You've seen some recovery in export volume due to the depreciation of the yen, which made Japanese exporters recover competitiveness, such as in autos, shipbuilding... I think there is a recovery in export activity in Japan," he added.
The figures showed Japan's crude oil imports for August rose 53.8 percent from a year earlier, mainly due to an increase in global prices.
A Finance Ministry official said the ministry was keeping a close watch on movements in international crude oil prices and their impact on the surplus.
Nobuyuki Saji, senior economist at Nikko Research Center, said the yen's weakness against the dollar had begun to restrict the pace of increase of import volume.

Andrew Shipley, an economist at Schroders Japan, said the slowdown in imports was the main reason the surplus was not much smaller. He added, however, that import demand should increase again once industrial production picked up in the fourth quarter of the year.

He also said a recovery in consumption on the back of improving labour market conditions should fuel demand for foreign goods, particularly U.S.-made cars, and this would mean the surplus would continue to drop quite rapidly in the second half of this year.
"We think it is going to fall faster. We are looking at a 50 percent year-on-year decline," he said.

Other economists have predicted that the pace of shrinkage in the surplus would slow towards the year's end, reflecting the yen's sharp decline against the dollar from its level a year ago, something that has helped manufacturers regain some competitiveness abroad.
The trade data is reported by the Ministry only in yen terms. Conversions are at the current dollar/yen rate of 110 yen.
